items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I would perform in Harold’s group, actually I’d been performing with Harold long before I went to New York you know.

ctx.x: Okay. So I started up again. Let me ask you about Tribe. Would bands come to you, groups of musicians, with a finished audio recording and then you would take that and put it out on your label? Or did you work with the musicians from the get-go?

No, well I was working with a cadre of musicians. I was working with Phil Ranelin, which we started a partnership, Tribe Records. The magazine was different. But I needed some help on administrative stuff so I incorporated with Phil and myself as Tribe Records. And then Marcus — I used Marcus Belgrave and Harold McKinney basically was the network. Because we was playing in each other’s group. I was playing in Marcus’s group, me and Phil was playing in Marcus’s group, was playing in Harold’s group, you know, and…

groove. And then a guy from Ann Arbor, Ron Brooks submitted some music and David Durrah out of Cleveland submitted some music. So anyway that’s how that started, and then we distributed this music by independent distributors that was happening all over America, independent distributors, they wanted to distribute their own product and have their own catalogue as opposed to working for Atlantic Records or a big corporation. This was like an independent revolution as it were, you know, in the 60s. Everybody was…

items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Harold McKinney wrote that a little later you know.

ctx.x: Yeah. Because on that cut I heard it. I’m not sure which trumpet player it was but at any rate it was like a little road map of different styles and I wondered what the music looked like because there was times when everybody was playing together like you wrote a musical marker. And I almost pictured the recording session like maybe people were improvising, it was freer, and then you’re cuing in — okay we’re moving on here. Am I like hallucinating here?

No, no, back in the — the way we played, when we did a concert, in fact the record is like from a concert. In other words when we did a concert it was a continuous music, going from one tune to the next. And we started with “Mary had an Abortion” and that was real fast tempo right? Real fast tempo. And the chorus was going down in minor thirds, like a B flat major to G major to E major to D flat major, repeated over and over and over again, and we’re writing lines on this. We’d play [scats] and we kept on playing…

the tune, music keeps developing. We had different pieces over the years, we had, we’d revisit these tunes and add different things to it, different tunes and different melodies, lyrics and whatnot, changed a different chords and whatnot. You keep adding to it. Now after “Where Am I” it goes into a tune called “Angry Young Man” which is in 6/8. But the same changes as “Mary Had an Abortion” but it’s in 6/8 now. Instead of [claps fast] we had [claps slow] we had 6/8 [scats] Same thing [scats] it’s the same format…
